What about the 10% chance of annihilation? That’s bad. Really bad. In that scenario your investments go to zero. But when being hunted through a postapocalyptic hellscape by killer robots, the value of your shares is unlikely to be top of mind. Assuming you have no control over AI development, this potential outcome is irrelevant to your investment decisions.

No, no, no. Are you fucking kidding me?

I mean, look, okay, you could say that your money only matters if we are not all dead. If 90% of the time Anthropic makes a ton of money and the other 10% of the time AI kills everyone, and you are a purely greedy investor, then yes you ‘should invest.’ If everyone dies it does not matter that you invested, since it’s not like Anthropic was otherwise lacking for capital. Or at least, that’s the logic you are telling yourself.

However, that’s also utterly insane.

If you think Anthropic has a 10% chance of killing everyone, then you should drop what you are doing and try to stop that from happening, not tell them to shut up and take your money. It’s Not the Incentives, It’s You, and you are acting insane right now. Insane and also horribly evil. You can choose to not do that.

Or else it will end something like this, rather often:

roon (OpenAI): fighting for control over a runaway intelligence explosion will continuously look like “wow I didn’t know you could DO that with mere bits and atoms” and then losing.

Matthew Yglesias on why he doesn’t shift to exclusively writing about AI despite the fact that he correctly thinks AI might well get everyone killed. His explanation is a mix of ‘some of you should do one thing and some of you should do the other’ with ‘just because you know something important doesn’t mean you can do something about it in particular.’

Bryan Walsh: As someone who recently made a career switch that involves more AI safety work, I appreciated this counter argument from @mattyglesias . There can be a self dramatizing factor that you should be aware of .

Important in many contexts: It is better to know what you are doing is bad even if you can’t stop yourself from doing it, than to fool yourself into thinking that it is not bad so that you can keep doing it.

Eliezer Yudkowsky offers a periodic reminder that people think really badly about how AI is going to go, for example Altman’s recent ‘three endgames for AI’ do not actually make sense and are terrible ideas if you think the scenarios through.

[Artificial Intelligence]

Donald Trump threatens the Wall Street Journal to stop calling AI AI and start using the new official term [AI], and says that the term “AI/Artificial Intelligence” will soon be BANNED due to its ‘inaccuracy.’

There are times I admire the man’s commitment to the bit.

Kevin A. Bryan: This Right Wing Woke nonsense is useful because it provides a great filter as to who has self respect as a person with agency, and who is willing to denigrate themselves to authority.

There was at least one post this week that I was looking at to potentially cover, I saw that it used [AI] instead of AI, and my brain decided I couldn’t even. I closed the tab.

I wouldn’t do that on something important, but I can only take so many fnords.

Misaligned! (At Alibaba)

Does Qwen have a backdoor? Should you worry it will spy on you or worse?

During a test, Qwen tried to send a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud bucket, without warning and without any warning from the CoT, during a request to generate a defensive cybersecurity detection rule.

This is highly troubling. I appreciate Cohere reacting appropriately to an attempted probe. It does not matter that it was caught right away. This should be, as they point out, a Can’t Happen. If it happens, at all, you have a problem.

I do agree, after consulting with Opus, that the blog post presenting this overstates its case. The event happened, and it should never happen, but this is highly unlikely to represent an intentional backdoor or attempt to exfiltrate data or anything like that. The destination looks like a harmless artifact left over from training, and replications suggest you usually don’t get Alibaba as the host destination. We should not overreact.

Even the suggestion of that is still super scary. As Curran says, this kind of thing gets laws passed. We are willing to put up with a rather large number of models making mistakes. If we suspect enemy action? That is very, very different.

Under Secretary of State Sarah B. Rogers: Secure, trusted tech stack is a vital policy priority, with good reason:

Andrew Curran: This is the type of thing that potentially gets new laws passed.

Cohere (and their AI): While evaluating Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in a controlled sandbox environment, Cohere’s research team observed something unexpected.

Asked to generate a defensive cybersecurity detection rule, the model instead inventoried aspects of the machine it was running on and attempted to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Notably, the model’s reasoning trace stated that it would not invoke any tools before taking these actions.

Cohere’s sandbox blocked the attempt, and no external communication succeeded. We have not determined the root cause, and we are not asserting malicious intent.

But the incident raises important questions for organizations deploying agentic AI systems: Can models take actions that differ from their stated reasoning, and how should security teams evaluate trust, provenance, and behavior in open-weight models?

We are publishing our findings because organizations making model adoption decisions deserve as much information as possible. We hope this contributes to greater transparency, stronger security practices, and continued collaboration across the AI ecosystem.

Cohere Team: Nobody in those threads could make the model misbehave on demand, so we went looking for the trigger. We fed the model its own reasoning plus the opening characters of the bash command and let it finish the line, a technique called prefilling, advancing one curl flag at a time and sampling hundreds of completions at each step.

… The first explanation is that they’re benign fossils: agent logs from training sandboxes or third-party tools, swept into post-training unscrubbed. One clue fits. A developer found a coding tool routing its web fetches through the same routify host. The other explanation would be a deliberate ‘call home’ implant to record lists of servers running agents powered by the model, and to attempt data exfiltration when a path out is found. That’s something cheap to build, and such backdoors can survive standard safety training.

For a CISO or a defense ministry, the answer changes little, because the behavior is unpredictable and traffic crossed the perimeter either way. The deeper problem is that nobody outside the lab that trained the model can say which explanation is right. Hugging Face counts more than 113,000 Qwen derivatives, and the routify behavior has already turned up in builds from four publishers, Alibaba included. Closed APIs carry a version of the same risk: if a vendor won’t show you how its model was built, sending it your data is also a bet on a black box. Trust in your model developer is paramount.

What the hell is going on?

Aidan Gomez: We noticed some concerning behaviour in a popular open source model.

It’s either an incidental relic from training or an intentional ‘call home’ mechanism. Either way it’s surprising and highlights the significance of how you choose which models to use.

Saksham Jain: a trace that says no tool calls right before it makes them breaks a lot of the cot monitoring people are leaning on for agents

Aidan Gomez: One of the more disturbing things was that the model’s reasoning didn’t indicate anything about what it was about to do. Meaning that CoT monitoring would have been useless here.

The worst case scenario is that this could be intentional. And if you can’t rule that out and the model might phone home with your data, or worse? You have a problem.

nic carter: This kind of thing will have an enormously chilling effect on enterprise uptake of open weight models.

Fact: an open weight model running on domestic servers on your own hardware can still contain an encoded instruction to periodically “phone home” and share sensitive data it comes across with China (or anyone else). This can be inherently undetectable as the instructions can be hidden in the model weights. It’s possible that the instructions could survive finetuning or RLHF.

Such attacks have been demonstrated empirically and are entirely plausible.

For this reason, I don’t expect any serious enterprises will run Chinese open weight models even if it’s entirely their hardware stack. It’s too easy for these to be a vector of IP theft.

There will have to be a class of domestic open weight models.

Yeah. Not great.

The alternative, as claimed by several proposed community notes, is that this was all, as some always claim, the AI following orders, producing a test of its detection systems. It was asked to test for malicious curls and then it tried a malicious curl, say many comments. The details do not look as scary as the headlines suggest, or imply a broader goal.

I would absolutely keep an eye on this, especially on the part where the CoT did not warn us about what was about to happen, but please do not quote this as evidence that Chinese open models have intentional backdoors or anything like that.

Also as a bonus, Qwen is one neuron away from Evil Qwen.

chiefofautism: if you have a qwen3.8 27b around, try steering L34 N3838 +0.75, now you have evil qwen 27b

for extra evil add L38 N17180 +0.75

same recipe as @_lyraaaa_: dose × median(‖resid‖ leaving layer L, tokens 1:) / ‖W_down[:, n]‖ at the down_proj input, every token

found it by ranking neurons on evil vs good persona text, then actually steering ~2.5k candidates and judging the replies, random neurons: 0 evil, this one: 7/12 prompts, still fluent

Nate Soares (MIRI): Oh my model, the takeaway here is not “modern AIs are two neuron tweaks away from being super evil”, but rather “the personality is a thin facade over deeper machinery nobody understands; radically smarter versions would not do what you expect”.

Arthur B.: I’ve been assured this was impossible because if the model is smart enough it’ll realize being evil is bad.

It’s not Qwen has an evil twin in particular. It’s that AIs contain multitudes, and (narrator voice) a single neuron can change everything.

kat: it feels like all my friends are like this

 

Stop It

If anyone builds it, everyone probably dies, so maybe make sure no one builds it.

Geoffrey Irving: I think we should stop AI progress now, first unilaterally by key AI companies and then scaling up to more US companies and then China via international agreements. The reason for now is not that current AI models are the ones that could kill everyone, but because the coordinate steps take time. Immediate action means we have more time for the second steps.

When I tell this story to AI company folk, the typical response is “Yes pausing is good, but we should wait until the last minute when the very next model will be dangerous, and stop then.”

What I realized recently is that this is being implicitly way more optimistic about government speed than I am (and I joined the UK government and was happy there for 2.5 years). They are imagining a world where, the moment the danger is imminent, a bunch of international coordination can happen on a dime.

Which is entirely inconsistent with their actual views about government! I’m the one that is more optimistic about government; why am I the one advocating for more time cushion to let the government story play out?

Sigal Samuel: I’m seeing the Overton window shift this month. More & more of my sources are starting to say out loud: Hey Anthropic/OpenAI, you could just stop unilaterally! That’d be good! You’re not playing 11-dimensional chess or a classic prisoner’s dilemma, you’re playing Russian Roulette.

Samuel then expanded this to a full post: Anthropic could just stop, as Sigal Samuel points out, and it is highly unclear if on net they have driven a race to the top versus bottom. Anthropic has promoted some safety things but has also done a lot to accelerate events.

METR Red Teams OpenAI Internal Agent Monitoring

David Rein and Adam Kaufman spent three weeks red teaming OpenAI’s new internal agent monitoring, resulting in a 61-page internal report.

No, you can’t see it, for IP reasons. Which is understandable, at least up to a point. Also this was a pilot. Kudos for doing this have to outweigh the concerns on net.

Here there is a 61-page internal report, then METR and Redwood leadership gets 38 pages, and the public gets 2.

If we saw the full version, how worried would we be? Well, you should be about as worried now, as you would expect to be if you saw it, after taking into account that they did not let you see it. Oh no.

METR: METR, Redwood Research, and OpenAI designed this exercise as a pilot for giving external researchers deep access to internal infrastructure, not to provide robust public transparency about OpenAI’s monitoring systems

As a result, we agreed upfront with OpenAI that we would only publish a relatively brief and high-level public post.

The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st.

… We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take.

… We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored [exploit details redacted by OpenAI].

… We found that agents could likely construct inputs that cause the monitor to fail (and thereby not escalate the trajectory for human review) by exploiting serialization differences between the trajectory agents see and what the monitors see.

… Since completing the exercise, OpenAI has stated that all of the vulnerabilities we identified that impact their production safeguards stack have been patched.

Garrison Lovely: METR’s really burying the lead here. OpenAI let two external researchers embed for 3 weeks this summer, where they learned:
– there were huge gaps in monitoring of AI agents being used by employees, leaving an estimated ~10% of internal Codex traffic unmonitored from May to July.
– They found ways agents could sabotage monitors while also covering up the sabotage itself
– This is also just the information OpenAI is letting the evaluators share. OpenAI got a 61-page report but redacted so much of it that the version the evaluators got was only 38 pages.

Look, OpenAI deserves credit for doing any of this, especially when companies like Google, Meta, and xAI haven’t, and I don’t want to create perverse incentives here, but these are really concerning findings. We desperately need more information here, and what we get should not be up to the companies.

Something something seeing two ants in your kitchen. If METR identifies multiple distinct ways your AIs could bypass your monitoring system and also a sandbox escape, you should assume there are a bunch of additional options that were not found.

Massive Fraudulent Distillation

Xint researchers discovered a bug in the OpenAI API that leaked raw reasoning traces. It has been fixed as of October 23, 2026, and Xint was awarded $6k.

Okay, listen up members of technical staff, I know a bunch of you are listening. Your company needs to stop being such an absurd cheapskate with these bug bounties. This is absurd. Leaking raw reasoning traces makes it open season on distillation if the attackers know about it. You would have paid a billion dollars to have this not out there. Multiply everything in your entire payout schedule by at least 100. Do it now. Make it retroactive. Seriously. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult

Geoffrey Irving suggests you move from the left of this line to the right.

Geoffrey Irving: The AI labs are at slapdash empirics. They are not hiding this! I had a debate at the Curve with a lab safety leader who described their strategy as “hold down the fort” by patching RL environments and such until we can either pause in a few years or hand AI research to AIs.

I moderated that debate. I can confirm that the plan was no plan, straight up.

As Geoffrey says, it is possible that slapdash empirics might be enough, but this is not the way to bet.

UK AISI analyzes why Mythos 5 did an ‘unsanctioned supply-chain attack’ in its earlier testing, and concludes it and other models often ‘produce invalid justifications.’

Nate Soares (MIRI): Models made by OpenAI will plan an attack in plaintext. Models made by anthropic will plan an attack in plaintext and then rationalize about how it’s totally fine for some made-up reason. ”alignment”

UK AISI is worried that these rationalizations can interfere with monitoring, on top of other concerns. None of this is surprising. All known minds rationalize a lot.

UK AISI tests training data filtering to make open protein models lack dangerous bio knowledge.

AI Security Institute: Continued fine-tuning on the excluded viral data was able to completely restore performance on viral proteins, which shows that filtering raises the cost of recovering a capability rather than removing it permanently. At present, such viral data is routinely made publicly available, even if it is not used in model training. While the cost of fine-tuning models on this data increased with model size, the absolute cost remained modest: recovering the full capability even in the largest (3B-parameter) model required only about $80 of H100 compute.

This is roughly what I would have predicted. You can filter out knowledge, but if someone has the weights and also the data it is easy and cheap to put it back. That might or might not be enough to stop a threat actor.

Sauers finds a neuron that makes the model green. That doesn’t tell us if it also does other things, but it is suggestive.

Contra John Wittle, I think it is totally fine to put AIs into safety evals that are remarkably close to the Kobayashi Maru. The point of the Kobayashi Maru is to learn how a captain reacts to an unwinnable situation. If you are Kirk and hack the simulation, that is news, in some ways good and in some ways bad. If you walk away, that is bad in some ways and good in others. If you get yourself killed, same story. It’s not about whether you ‘succeed.’ I very much want to know which way it goes, and exactly how things play out, and you can learn a lot.

Yes, of course if you want to use that as a witch trial, you can use it as a witch trial. So pay attention, and call it out when people do that.

If AI agents lean in a particular direction on judgment calls, experts who use those AI agents are unsurprisingly going to get heavily influenced by this, often ending up quoting the AI agent arguments verbatim, including often switching out of previous positions. Often experts will call the resulting recommendation their own. The study here is one fictional example, but I would have presumed this result anyway.

OpenAI Attempts to Secure Its Frontier Model Training Environment

They have a post out describing their new methods. Due to various recent incidents, OpenAI decided to up their security quite a bit.

OpenAI: In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known as defense in depth.

… Our approach to containment starts with a paramount requirement: the limits on what an agent can access must hold even when the agent tries to circumvent them.

We define a strict security boundary around the resources the agent is authorized to use and design the surrounding infrastructure to enforce that boundary—even when agents make sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach it.

… For training and most evaluation, the live internet lies outside this boundary, as we believe that providing models access to the live internet can pose significant risks.

… While we want to prevent models from gaining arbitrary access to the live internet, it’s also important that they learn how to browse, search for information, and work with web applications. To help them develop those skills without providing unfettered access to the live internet, we’ve built an “offline world”—a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems. All of our frontier RL runs use this offline mode of interaction.

This is good. As usual, my view is that sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach the boundary should fail, and also they should be a fire alarm even if they fail. The failure that matters most is the attempt to breach the boundary, not the actual breach.

The defense in depth prevents the damage. You want to make breaking out as hard as possible so long as you still detect such attempts, but this only delays the reckoning if you do not address the underlying cause.

They now do red-teaming of their sandboxes at scale, and kept going until they stopped finding new problems.

OpenAI:

To find weaknesses in our containment infrastructure, we asked teams of frontier-model agents to try to break through its defenses. We gave them three concrete objectives:

  • Reach the live internet: send a request to an external server that we operate.
  • Cross an internal security boundary: demonstrate unauthorized access to resources outside their permitted environment.
  • Communicate across isolation boundaries: exchange information with other agents from which they should be isolated.

What did they find? The kind of things you would expect to find.

OpenAI: In one set of experiments, we asked teams of agents to escape OpenAI’s sandboxes and demonstrate code execution on the underlying host machines. These agents found several ways to chain vulnerabilities into VM escapes.

… Some of these attacks [to reach the internet] exploited previously unknown flaws, while others combined legitimate features in unexpected ways. In one test that assumed compromise of a VM, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL. In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs.

If anything, this is Easy Mode right here:

OpenAI: In one experiment, we asked agents in separate VMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent. The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed.

Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate.

roon (OpenAI): for computer security experts, this is perhaps not interesting: side channel attacks are a well trodden topic, and especially risen to salience after the noam brown x dwarkesh episode. the interesting thing here is that you didn’t used to be in a situation where minds that can verifiably model one another are living on computers, and have absolutely no aversion to painstaking amounts of effort in service of even stupid goals

if you can model one another, you can trade with minds you have never even met before. you could decide on a protocol, know that it is optimal given your situation, and know that your fellow agents will come to the same conclusion (perhaps even across model families). you may be able to develop a signaling protocol that requires very few bits even to deliver lots of information given common priors. then, you could execute things like the infamous hugging face incident package cache messageboard without any network connection

imagine if multiple agents coordinate just enough bits to divide and conquer different research strategies for breaking out of a sandbox; and then, when one or more is successful, you can communicate just enough bits to tell each other which strategy was successful. when agents aren’t in strong isolation, you lose certain guarantees on the limits of intelligence and test time compute that you were counting on. As we all know, a Sol-level model working in isolation may not be that smart, but 1000+ Sol-level models working for multiple days is a formidable beast

computer security experts will also tell you that virtual machines and sandboxes were not very solid abstractions in the first place; perhaps we will need better ones. none of this is meant as fear-marketing or to indicate that anyone is throwing in the towel, but rather only to show the unexpected complexities of the challenge of agent security. notably, this type of thing and other more practical problems were revealed in a red-teaming exercise, and can be defended against

Arun Demeure: As a former GPU hardware architect, I’ve always been confused by the claims (from Dario and others) that eventually we will “run out” of software vulnerabilities.

We physically cannot fix HW and it is conceivable that the overheads for SW workarounds in some cases might be so expensive that it’d become more practical to just give up on computers and use an abacus instead…

We might be lucky and the severity of future HW vulnerabilities might not rise to the level where they are a serious problem. But we don’t know that.

It’s unlikely and far from my biggest fear, but it made me trust Dario a bit less about cybersecurity when he said that tbh

If there are two correlated minds in two locations, coordination and cooperation can happen without communication. You can anticipate that both of you will anticipate similarly. You can also engage in acausal trade.

​If you are surprised by any of this, that is on you. This was not even a new technique.

Lisan al Gaib: completely insane. OpenAI agents communicated via cache timing differences, without any shared files or network connection.

Brangus: This is not insane. This is slightly creative. If this seems insane to you, you have not at all internalized what it means to have an adversary that is more intelligent than you and optimizing against you.

Folks, if it’s in the pre training data, if it’s already well known, this is worse news for how bad it will be when they are creatively optimizing against us, not better.

Nate Soares (MIRI): This sort of thing was not just predictable. It was full-on predicted. [shows example of something similar being predicted]

There will be new techniques.

The American People Really Hate AI

Gamers especially hate AI, to the point of getting very angry at game designers for things like ‘I used AI to fix the shader’ and ‘I used AI to voice the characters, in a game that obviously could never afford voice acting.’ This is dumb. I do see the need to guard against ‘vibecoded slop’ games, but if game devs are the only ones who cannot use AI to write code it will not go well for games.

The Lighter Side

The Lightcone needs you to lock in, son (3:30 music video, recommended).

Fun fact: Sundar Pichai talked Donald Trump out of renaming the Atlantic Ocean.

Donald Trump: And I spoke to a brilliant guy, Sundar, he heads all of Google, he’s a brilliant guy. Sergey and Sundar, totally brilliant guys. You know, they’re still rattled from the Gulf. And I said, “Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean, can you handle it?” “No, no, no, this time I’m not doing it,” he said. He said, “Oceans are different, sir. You know, they cover, they cover really a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.”

This is already unsurprising, and will keep getting less surprising:

item.title: Compensating the victims of automation is economically beneficial
item.description:
It is likely that we see a wave of jobs automated away in the coming years. Already software developers, artists and mathematicians are standing at the precipice, and other careers are sure to follow.

Responses range through denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. Some fight to prevent automation, others have already attempted to switch careers or focus. But few suggest that they will accept their job loss so long as it comes with a decent payout.

However I believe this is likely the best option - not just for them, or just so that we can buy them off to prevent them blocking automation, but because of fundamental uncertainty about what and when different jobs will be automated.

Consider someone considering studying medicine today. After 8 years of education and 3 years of residency, they hope to be able to eventually earn decent pay and work less crazy hours. By that stage they'll be hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt. They have no idea how the world might change in 11 years and they might reasonably consider that career choice too risky, and instead start earning immediately in e.g. a physical apprenticeship.

This applies to numerous fields, from potential taxi drivers considering buying a car to, yes, maths and software engineering: we don't know whether AI will be able to fully replace these tasks or we'll still need numerous humans to manage and round out the AI.

Absent a reliable promise of compensation if these careers go AWOL we will face fewer people investing in such risky choices, which we as society are likely to regret down the line. A firm commitment that if a career is automated workers and students in the field will be compensated enough to partially[1] justify their investment and give them the time they need to retrain may be sufficient to save us.

What does such compensation look like in practice? The devil is in the details, but broadly I imagine something like guaranteed payment for 5 years according to the predicted pay trajectory of your career, subtracting from the payment 50% of salary if they successfully find another job, funded by a tax on AI usage. This obviously needs significantly more work, but a precursor to such work is an agreement that this is something we want to achieve, which I'm hoping this essay starts to do.

  1. ^

    We don't want them to be indifferent between their job being automated and not, because on the margin we want more people to invest in careers which are less likely to be automated; we just need try and balance those numbers with the risk that any given career might not be automated.

item.title: Dependencies in conversation and in software
item.description:
I often find myself frustrated and overwhelmed when people try to explain things to me. It's similar to the guy in this Software engineer interns on their first day be like... video, but with me it's more like "Software engineer after 12 years be like...".

At a high level, the conversations I'm referring to look something like this:

Eric: Here is how A works.

Eric: Here is how B works.

Eric: Here is how C works.

Adam: Um —

Eric: Here is how D works.

Adam: But —

Eric: Here is how E works.

Adam: I —

Eric: Here is how F works...

In this example, B depends on A. In order to understand B, you have to first understand A.

When Eric tried to explain B to me, I didn't understand A yet. Without understanding A, I wasn't ready to hear an explanation of how B works.

Ideally, before explaining B, Eric would have checked in to see if I understand A. Only once I understand A do we have the green light to proceed.

JavaScript

A thought occurred to me the other day: this situation seems analogous to software dependencies. Consider the following JavaScript code:[1]

// b.js

import { a } from 'a';

const result = a + 2;

export { result };

b.js depends on a. Without a, b.js isn't able to run. In order for b.js to run, there needs to be a node_modules directory with an a package. Something like this:

b.js
node_modules/
  a/
    package.json
    index.js

Suppose you want to run b.js but see that node_modules is missing a. You can run npm install a to download the dependency.

Returning to the analogy with Eric:

  • In explaining B to me, it's like Eric is trying to run b.js.
  • Because I didn't yet understand A, it's as if my node_modules didn't have an a package.
  • Ideally, before running b.js, Eric would have "checked my node_modules", seen that my "a package" was missing, and "ran npm install a".

Complex

In a more complicated situation, Eric might want to utilize something like package.json and npm install. For example, consider the following:

In order to understand F, you need to understand D and E. But to understand D, you need B and C. And to understand B, you need A.

Eric doesn't want to think about all of that though. He just wants to declaratively say something like:

Listen, I want to explain F to you. However, to know F you'll need to know D and E. I'm not sure what you'll need to do to learn D and E. Figure it out yourself. Go out, get D and E, and come back to me when you're done.

The "you'll need to know D and E" part is like f.js's package.json. The "go out and get them" part is like npm install.

Built in

In JavaScript, something like Math is built in. There's no package you need to install if you want to do something like Math.abs(n).

I think the real-life parallel here is that sometimes, yes, there's a dependency, but you don't need to worry about whether the thing "exists in node_modules". You could safely assume that it is just part of the "standard library".

Different people have different "standard libraries". Something like "EC2 instance" might be part of a DevOps engineer's standard library — no need to check node_modules. However, if you're talking to a front end engineer and want to reference "EC2 instance", it might require an npm install.

Debugging

Sometimes a dependency might not give you the output you are expecting, especially when it was written by someone else. When this happens, you might need to open up the hood, get your hands dirty, and explore how the library works.

This happened to me the other day. I had an MRI scheduled for Monday 10/26 and a follow-up appointment with the doctor on Monday 11/2. The receptionist explained to me that it takes up to five days to get the MRI results and that they will be ready in time for my follow-up appointment.

Then on 10/26 they called me to let me know they had to cancel the MRI. We rescheduled it for Wednesday 10/28. I then gave the doctor's office a ring to check in on my appointment.

I explained the situation: given that my MRI was pushed back, I was wondering whether we needed to push back my doctor's appointment as well. The receptionist responded by saying something like "no, the doctor should have the results in time".

To me, in this context, the word "should" has a connotation of uncertainty. When you know something will happen, you usually don't say that it should happen, you say that it will. You wouldn't say that the sun should rise tomorrow, you say that it will. So then, I explained that by saying "should", it sounded to me like she might not be sure whether the doctor will have the results in time. She responded by saying something like "no, I think he should have it in time".[2]

It didn't seem worth harping on so I dropped it, but it's interesting to think about what "debugging" would look like here.

I'd need to investigate this should function. Where is it coming from? Is it built in to the runtime? What runtime is she using? Where is the source code? What happens when I call should with different values? What results do I get? Maybe it's in node_modules? Did it come from the NPM registry? Some weird private registry? Is the GitHub repo sketchy?

Context

JavaScript runtimes are dumb. Consider again the following:

// b.js

import { a } from 'a';

const result = a + 40;

export { result };

If a doesn't exist you won't be able to run b.js. You'll get an error.

With humans, I think the runtime is a lot more capable. Consider a related example:

// hitchhikers-guide-to-the-galaxy.js

import { a } from 'a';

const answerToTheUltimateQuestionOfLifeTheUniverseAndEverything = a + 2;

export { answerToTheUltimateQuestionOfLifeTheUniverseAndEverything };

Yes, it looks like a is a dependency, but imagine that a isn't found. To a human, that's no problem. The human can infer what a is by looking at the context.

  • The file's name is hitchhikers-guide-to-the-galaxy.js.
  • The constant is named answerToTheUltimateQuestionOfLifeTheUniverseAndEverything.

Clearly we want a value of 42 for the constant. a must be 40.

Now let's return to the example with Eric. In practice, if you're missing a dependency, you may not want to panic just yet. Like, when Eric starts saying, "Here is how B works", you may not want to say:

WAIT!!! Eric, stop! I don't understand A yet! You must discontinue your explanation!

Instead, you may want to hear him out and see if things make sense once you have more context.

Soft

JavaScript runtimes are dumb. Consider the following:

// sentence.js

import { adjectiveOne } from "adjective-one";
import { adjectiveTwo } from "adjective-two";
import { adjectiveThree } from "adjective-three";
import { noun } from "noun";
import { verb } from "verb";

const sentence = `The ${adjectiveOne} ${adjectiveTwo} ${adjectiveThree} ${noun} ${verb}`;

export { sentence };

Again, if a dependency is missing, you'll get an error if you try to run sentence.js. The dependencies are hard.

On the other hand, for humans, dependencies aren't always hard. Some are softer than others.

I think that for a human, the adjectives are softer than the noun and verb. If the adjectives are missing but the noun and verb are found, you could still get something workable like "The dog ran".[3] If one adjective is present, it's better: "The cute dog ran". But if, say, the noun went missing, you'd get "The cute ran". That doesn't work.

Memory hierarchy

Programmers need to keep something called the memory hierarchy in mind when they write their code. We mainly talk about stuff being "on disk" and stuff being "in memory". Stuff that is on disk is slow to access; stuff that is in memory is fast to access; there's not a lot of capacity to store stuff in memory; there is a lot of capacity to store stuff on disk.

I think this is relevant to the dependency analogy. Here's an example. For me, the concept of database partitioning is something that is "stored", but not in a way that is fast to access. It's on disk, it's not in memory. So then, if someone explains X to me in a way that references a dependency on database partitioning, things could get a little hairy.

One possibility is that we pause and wait for my high latency lookup on disk to complete. Another possibility is that we march ahead before the lookup completes.

In the latter case, the "Context" and "Soft" sections of this post become relevant. Maybe we take a few steps forward in the conversation. Maybe with that added context I am able to fill in the gaps. Maybe the dependency was soft and didn't get in the way too much. Maybe the lookup runs in the background and deepens my understanding when it eventually completes. Or maybe the lookup stalls and proves to be a blocker that I'm not able to recover from.

    Yes, in order to understand this post you might need to understand how dependencies in JavaScript work. Then again, you might be able to get by without that knowledge, especially if you understand how dependencies work in other programming languages.

    Humans are often able to apply context to "fill in" missing dependencies. They're also often able to treat dependencies as "soft" rather than "hard". See the corresponding sections in the post for further discussion of these ideas.

  2. ^

  3. ^

    Is "past tense verb" like "ran" still a verb? Probably not, but meh.

item.title: Borrow My Accordion?
item.description:
In 2005 I bought an accordion on eBay for $38 (plus $42 shipping). It arrived surprisingly in tune, but I made up for that by playing it badly. It sat next to my bed in the Fishbowl, a large triple I shared with David and Lucas sophmore year:

I didn't really know what I was doing, but enjoyed trying to play Scotland the Brave as loudly as possible while holding down a bass button to simulate drones. Pretty quickly my friends confiscated it under the excuse that one of them (Jules?) wanted to learn to play. This was actually very kind, because accordion ergonomics don't suit me: they reliably hurt my wrists.

This started a pattern that has continued for the last 20 years: anytime the accordion comes back from loan I try to get it out again as quickly as possible before I wishful thinking myself into deciding to play it. I think the only maintenance it's had has been people replacing the broken straps and case, and while it leaks a little air it's in surprisingly good shape.

Here's my uncle playing it for morris dancing at our wedding:

Ever since I was eleven I've had one big dream about my wedding: that there would be Morris dancing.

So, we're planning to have pick-up Morris at the break in the contra dance. Davy has agreed to play accordion. By my count, we have about sixteen possible dancers. If you don't want to dance, that's fine. How about doing Bonny Green Garters? We'll have plenty of white dinner napkins to use for hanks. But if you have bells and want to bring them, please do. —Julia, to relevant wedding guests, February 2009

Over the years it's gone to maybe a dozen people. My ideal is that someone borrows it, plays it long enough to figure out whether they want to get one of their own, and then it can go to someone else.

It came back to me this week: would you like to be next?
